title: Book 9 — Calliope, Chapter 116
paragraphs: The tyrant of the province was Artaÿctes, a governor under Xerxes — a Persian, but a man of desperate and reckless character — who had also practiced deception on the king on his march against Athens, by taking away from Elaius the things belonging to Protesilaos son of Iphiclos. For at Elaius in the Chersonese there is the tomb of Protesilaos with a sacred precinct around it, where there were many treasures — gold and silver cups, bronze, robes, and other offerings — all of which Artaÿctes carried off as plunder, the king having granted them to him. He deceived Xerxes by saying to him something like this: “Master, here there is the house of a man, a Greek, who made an expedition against your land, met with his deserts, and was killed. I ask you to give me this man's house, so that everyone may learn not to make expeditions against your land.” By saying this, it was likely enough that he would persuade Xerxes to give him a man's house, not suspecting what was in his mind. When he said that Protesilaos had made an expedition against the king's land — understand that the Persians consider all Asia theirs and belonging to their reigning king. So when the things had been granted him, he brought them from Elaius to Sestos, sowed the sacred precinct for crops and occupied it as his own; and whenever he came to Elaius, he had intercourse with women in the inner sanctuary of the temple. And now he was being besieged by the Athenians, when he had made no preparation for a siege nor expected the Greeks to come; for they fell upon him, one might say, unavoidably.
